title: The Crown on the Red Carpet
rule: grab that crown with your bare hands, without touching the carpet
loophole: The king never said the carpet had to stay flat on the floor.

beats.voiceover: An old king tossed his solid gold crown dead-center onto a red carpet the size of a barn. "Whoever brings it back," he grinned, "rules this entire kingdom after me!"
beats.visual: An amused old king drops his shining gold crown into the dead center of a massive red carpet in a grand stone hall.

beats.voiceover: Sounds easy—until he dropped the catch. "Just one rule: grab that crown with your bare hands, without touching the carpet." Every edge was twenty feet from the gold. Three challengers stepped up.
beats.visual: The king holds up one finger pointing across the enormous red carpet while three eager challengers size up the distance.

beats.voiceover: The first was the kingdom's proudest knight. He sprinted like a bull and leaped fifteen feet through the air. He belly-flopped straight onto the wool while the whole court cracked up.
beats.visual: An armored knight leaps through the air and slides face-first across the red carpet as noblemen burst out laughing.

beats.voiceover: The second was a smug billionaire duke. He slammed a chest of gold beside the throne. "I just bought your carpet—it's my floor now!" The king grinned and pointed at the door.
beats.visual: A wealthy duke drops a heavy gold chest beside the throne and steps smugly toward the carpet while the king shakes his head.

beats.voiceover: The third was a teenage kitchen girl in a flour-dusted apron. Half the room snickered—until she calmly knelt on the bare stone edge and started rolling the carpet up like a giant sleeping bag. Turn by turn, the crown slid straight to her knees. She plucked it up and winked. The king burst out laughing—he'd never said the carpet had to stay flat.
beats.visual: A smiling kitchen girl kneels on the bare stone floor rolling up the red carpet as the gold crown slides right up to her hands.

title: The River and the Dry Feet
rule: cross my river with dry feet, no boat and no bridge
loophole: The king never said the river had to be crossed that day.

beats.voiceover: On the last crisp afternoon of autumn, a bored king dangled a heavy sack of gold beside a wide rushing river. He dared anyone in the crowd to win it.
beats.visual: A grinning king holds up a heavy sack of gold beside a wide, fast river framed by red and gold autumn trees.

beats.voiceover: "Simple test," he called out. "Cross my river with dry feet, no boat and no bridge—and every coin is yours!" Three bold men shoved to the front.
beats.visual: Three confident men step forward on the rocky riverbank staring out across the wide rushing current.

beats.voiceover: The first was a cocky soldier who laughed at the river. He hopped from boulder to boulder—until rock three's moss sent him splashing in up to his helmet.
beats.visual: A proud soldier slips on a mossy river rock and splashes straight into the rushing water up to his neck.

beats.voiceover: The second was a rich merchant who figured he'd cracked it. He bought the tallest warhorse around and rode proudly in. Halfway across, deep water filled both fancy boots.
beats.visual: A finely dressed merchant rides a massive horse into the river as deep water rises right over his tall leather boots.

beats.voiceover: The third was a sleepy old fisherman. He strolled down to the bank, sat on a log, and literally did nothing. The crowd groaned and went home. Autumn leaves blew away. Weeks passed. Thick winter snow covered the hills. One freezing January morning, he yawned, stood up, and strolled straight across the solid ice. The king hadn't once said he had to cross today.
beats.visual: On a snowy winter morning, a grinning old fisherman strolls casually across the thick frozen white river while the amazed king watches.

title: The Candle That Lasted Longest
rule: whoever's candle lasts the longest gets the whole farm
loophole: The father never said the candle had to be lit.

beats.voiceover: An aging farmer had three fiercely competitive sons, one massive family farm, and the weirdest contest in the county. One windy evening, he handed each boy an identical white candle and a single match.
beats.visual: An old farmer sets three identical white candles and three matches across a wooden kitchen table in front of his three eager sons.

beats.voiceover: "One fair rule," the old man said with a tiny smirk. "Whoever's candle lasts the longest gets the whole farm." Then he blew out the kitchen lamp and headed straight up to bed.
beats.visual: The smirking old farmer walks up the wooden stairs to bed while his three sons stare down at their candles in the dim room.

beats.voiceover: The first son was pure pride. He struck his match immediately and marched onto the windy porch waving his flame high. One gust hit—in forty minutes, nothing was left but wax.
beats.visual: A boastful young man holds a flickering candle high on a windy porch as wax streams fast down his hand.

beats.voiceover: The second son thought he was the family genius. He lit his wick, tucked it inside a deep glass jar away from drafts, and guarded it all night. Right before dawn, it sputtered dead.
beats.visual: A focused young man sits at a dark table watching a tiny candle stub flicker out inside a glass jar before sunrise.

beats.voiceover: And the third son? He looked at his candle, looked at his match, shrugged—and tucked the unlit candle under his pillow before going to sleep. At breakfast, he laid a brand-new candle beside his father's coffee. The old man burst out laughing and slid him the deed. He'd never said to light it.
beats.visual: At the sunny breakfast table, the youngest son hands a completely untouched white candle to his laughing father.
